definitions.definition: "Aggrieved woman" means — in relation to a workplace, a woman, of any age whether employed or not, who alleges to have been subjected to any act of sexual harassment by the respondent; in relation to a dwelling place or house, a woman of any age who is employed in such a dwelling place or house.
definitions.plain_english: An 'aggrieved woman' is any woman who claims she has been sexually harassed at a workplace, regardless of her age or whether she is officially employed there. For homes or residential premises, it refers to any woman of any age who works in that household. This definition is intentionally broad so that women in all kinds of work situations — formal or informal — can seek protection and file a complaint.
real_world_examples: A 28-year-old software engineer at an IT company in Bengaluru alleges that her male manager repeatedly made sexually coloured remarks during team meetings — she qualifies as an aggrieved woman even before any inquiry begins.

A 45-year-old domestic worker employed as a cook in a private household in Mumbai alleges that the male employer touched her inappropriately — she qualifies as an aggrieved woman in relation to the dwelling place.

A 19-year-old college intern (unpaid) at a media firm in Delhi alleges that a senior journalist demanded sexual favours in exchange for a positive performance review — she qualifies as an aggrieved woman even though she receives no salary.

A 35-year-old freelance consultant visiting a corporate client's office in Chennai for a one-day assignment alleges she was shown pornographic content by a client employee — she qualifies as an aggrieved woman despite not being a permanent employee of that organisation.

A 22-year-old contractual nurse at a private hospital in Hyderabad alleges repeated unwelcome physical contact by a senior doctor — she qualifies as an aggrieved woman under the workplace limb of the definition.

A 55-year-old part-time sweeper employed through a placement agency at a residential apartment in Pune alleges verbal sexual harassment by a male resident — she qualifies as an aggrieved woman in relation to the dwelling place.
what_it_covers: A permanent or regular female employee of any organisation who alleges sexual harassment at her workplace.
An unpaid intern, trainee, apprentice, or volunteer woman who alleges sexual harassment at the premises where she works or visits in the course of her duties.
A female domestic worker — whether full-time, part-time, temporary, or employed through an agency — who alleges sexual harassment in a private household.
A woman visiting a workplace (e.g., a client, vendor, or job applicant) who alleges sexual harassment during that visit.
A contractual or daily-wage woman worker who alleges sexual harassment, regardless of whether her employer is aware of her deployment at that site.
what_it_excludes: A male person alleging sexual harassment — the definition is expressly restricted to women only.
A woman who alleges sexual harassment in a purely personal/social setting entirely unconnected to any workplace or domestic employment relationship.

A female employer or household member who is not in an employment relationship at the relevant dwelling place — family members of the employer are explicitly excluded from the domestic worker category and the dwelling-place limb.
A woman whose allegation relates to conduct by another person that does not constitute 'sexual harassment' as defined under Section 2 of the Act.
A transgender person or male individual even if they identify with a gender covered under other laws — POSH Act's definition is confined to 'woman' as understood under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a complainant qualifies as an 'aggrieved woman' is the threshold condition that activates the entire complaints mechanism under the Act — only an aggrieved woman can file a complaint under Section 9, triggering mandatory inquiry obligations on the Internal Committee or Local Committee under Sections 11–13, interim relief provisions under Section 12, and employer duties under Section 19. If this definition does not apply, no committee is obligated to inquire, and no penalties or recommendations under Sections 13–15 and 18 can be invoked.

definitions.definition: "appropriate Government" means — in relation to a workplace which is established, owned, controlled or wholly or substantially financed by funds provided directly or indirectly by the Central Government or the Union territory administration, the Central Government; by the State Government, the State Government; in relation to any workplace not covered under sub-clause (i) and falling within its territory, the State Government.
definitions.plain_english: The 'appropriate Government' refers to whichever government — Central or State — has authority over a particular workplace under the POSH Act. If the workplace is run or funded by the Central Government or a Union Territory, the Central Government is the appropriate government. For all other workplaces within a State's boundaries, the State Government takes on this role.
real_world_examples: A woman employed at a Central Government ministry in New Delhi files a complaint of sexual harassment — here the Central Government is the appropriate Government responsible for monitoring compliance and notifying the District Officer.

An employee at a private IT company in Bengaluru, Karnataka, faces sexual harassment — the Karnataka State Government is the appropriate Government for that workplace and is responsible for publicising the Act and overseeing implementation.

A worker at a public sector undertaking like ONGC (funded by the Central Government) in Gujarat faces harassment — the Central Government is the appropriate Government, even though the workplace is physically located in a State.

A domestic worker employed in a household in Mumbai files a complaint — the Maharashtra State Government acts as the appropriate Government since private dwelling places fall under the residual State Government category.

An employee of a Union Territory administration office in Puducherry is harassed — the Central Government (acting through the Union Territory administration) is the appropriate Government for that workplace.

A teacher at a State-government-funded school in Rajasthan reports sexual harassment — the Rajasthan State Government is the appropriate Government responsible for notifying the District Officer and monitoring compliance.
what_it_covers: Workplaces established, owned, or controlled by the Central Government, such as central ministries, departments, and central public sector enterprises.
Workplaces wholly or substantially financed directly or indirectly by State Government funds, such as State government offices, State PSUs, and State-aided institutions.

All private sector workplaces, NGOs, hospitals, sports institutes, and dwelling places not covered under the Central Government category, which fall under the jurisdiction of the respective State Government.
Workplaces under Union Territory administrations, where the Central Government exercises the role of appropriate Government.
Government companies and corporations financed or controlled by the Central Government, such as BHEL, ONGC, or Indian Railways establishments.
what_it_excludes: Local bodies such as municipal corporations and panchayats, which are neither Central nor State Government entities and are separately referenced in the Act's definitions.
A workplace located in one State but falling under Central Government jurisdiction is excluded from that State Government's authority as 'appropriate Government' for that specific establishment.
International organisations or embassy workplaces operating in India, which are generally not subject to Indian governmental authority in the same manner.
Private households where domestic workers are employed are not governed by the Central Government under this definition, but fall under the State Government as the appropriate Government.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identification of the 'appropriate Government' determines which government body bears the legal obligation to notify District Officers under Section 5, monitor implementation of the Act, and take measures to publicise it under Sections 23 and 24. Misidentification of the appropriate Government can result in non-constitution of Local Complaints Committees, failure of enforcement mechanisms, and absence of accountability for compliance with the POSH Act.

definitions.definition: 'Chairperson' means the Chairperson of the Local Complaints Committee nominated under sub-section (1) of section 7.
definitions.plain_english: The Chairperson is the head of the Local Complaints Committee, which handles sexual harassment complaints in areas where there is no Internal Committee (such as for domestic workers or workers in the unorganised sector). This person is a woman nominated by the District Officer from among eminent individuals in the field of social work who are committed to the cause of women. The Chairperson leads the committee's proceedings, deliberations, and inquiry processes.
real_world_examples: A senior woman social activist working with an NGO in Pune is nominated by the District Collector as Chairperson of the Local Complaints Committee for Pune district to hear complaints from domestic workers alleging sexual harassment by their employers.

In a rural district in Rajasthan, a woman who has spent years advocating for gender rights at the block level is appointed Chairperson of the Local Committee to handle complaints from women employed in small unorganised shops and establishments with fewer than ten workers.

A well-known women's rights campaigner in Chennai is nominated as Chairperson of the Local Complaints Committee and presides over an inquiry involving a daily-wage female worker who filed a complaint against her supervisor at an unregistered construction site.

The District Officer in Bhopal nominates a retired female IAS officer with a background in social welfare as Chairperson of the Local Complaints Committee, and she chairs the inquiry into a complaint filed by a female home-based garment worker against her contractor.

In a metropolitan ward in Kolkata, the District Officer nominates a prominent women's rights lawyer as Chairperson of the Local Committee to oversee a complaint lodged by a part-time domestic worker who alleged sexual harassment by a household employer.
what_it_covers: A woman from the field of social work who is eminent and committed to the cause of women, nominated by the District Officer to head the Local Complaints Committee under Section 7(1)(a).

The presiding authority of the Local Complaints Committee who leads inquiries into sexual harassment complaints from women in areas or sectors not covered by an Internal Committee, including domestic workers and workers in the unorganised sector.
An individual who holds the highest decision-making and procedural authority within the Local Complaints Committee, responsible for conducting fair inquiries and recommending appropriate action.
what_it_excludes: The Presiding Officer of the Internal Complaints Committee constituted under Section 4, who is a separate statutory role defined under a different provision and governs complaints within organised workplaces with ten or more employees.
Any male individual, since Section 7 expressly requires the Chairperson to be nominated from amongst eminent women in the field of social work.
A woman who, though otherwise qualified, has not been formally nominated by the District Officer under sub-section (1) of Section 7, as the role is not self-assumed or employer-appointed.
Members of the Local Committee who are nominated under Section 7(1)(b) or 7(1)(c), as they hold a different, subordinate role to that of the Chairperson.

real_world_examples: A software engineer on a third-party vendor's payroll who works daily at an IT company's office in Bengaluru is an 'employee' of that workplace, even though her salary is paid by the vendor and not the IT company.

A freelance graphic designer engaged on an ad hoc project basis by a Delhi-based media house is covered as an 'employee' since ad hoc and contract workers are explicitly included in the definition.

A part-time beautician working at a small home-based salon in Mumbai with fewer than ten employees is harassed by a co-worker. With no Internal Committee in place, she submits her complaint to the Local Committee of her district.

A contract worker engaged through a staffing agency in a manufacturing unit has no formal service rules applicable to them; in such a case, the inquiry and consequent action shall be conducted in the manner prescribed under the rules framed under the POSH Act, 2013.

A woman athlete training at a government-run sports complex in Pune is harassed by her coach — a sports institute or stadium used for training is expressly covered as a workplace.
